items.title: How wildfire litigation became big business in America
items.summary_raw: On a November morning in 2018, the foothills of the Sierra Nevada were primed to burn. Northern California had received little rainfall, and the grasses and shrubs above the town of Paradise were bone dry. Humidity levels were dangerously low as winds up to 40 miles per hour gusted downslope toward the 26,000-person community. When a live wire broke free from a 99-year-old transmission tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric Co., Paradise stood little chance. The arcing wire ignited the brush below to start the Camp Fire, which claimed the lives of 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 structures in a matter of hours, charring whole neighborhoods to displace tens of thousands of people. It was the deadliest wildfire in California’s history. But another metric would later come to define the fire that destroyed Paradise. Thousands of victims sued PG&E. The utility eventually agreed to settle their claims for $13.5 billion in compensation for the Camp Fire, as well as other blazes ignited by its equipment in Northern California in 2017 and 2018. It was one of the largest civil settlements for an environmental disaster in U.S. history, driving the company to bankruptcy and demonstrating that utilities could be held liable for huge sums when faulty equipment ignites conflagrations. The settlement sparked a wave of lawsuits against utilities implicated in wildfire ignitions across the country. Today, wildfire litigation is a multibillion-dollar business in the U.S., with more…

items.title: Vladimír Mertlík: Veverky místo milenek a plyšáci na dovolenou. Česká politika připomíná zoologickou zahradu

Zatímco politici budují vztahy se zvířaty, premiér ruší reformu školního stravování. Děti podle něj nemají dostávat vnucovanou quinou, ale hlavně jídlo, které jim chutná. items.title: New net-zero community will become Michigan’s first virtual power plant
items.summary_raw: Mitch Hall and his wife, Lori, live in one of the most sustainable communities in the U.S. Their town house is among a few dozen residences constructed so far at Veridian at County Farm , a fossil-fuel-free, net-zero-energy development in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Homes here make about as much solar energy as they consume, with the help of batteries that save solar power for use in the evenings. Now, the couple is eager to share the benefits of their clean energy infrastructure with the wider grid. In the coming weeks, Veridian households can enroll in Michigan’s first residential pilot of a virtual power plant ; Detroit-based utility DTE Energy will then be able to remotely control the network of residents’ home batteries to inject their stored solar power onto the grid when operators need it most. “This pilot is an opportunity to test an approach that could ultimately provide a lower-cost way to meet growing energy needs and strengthen reliability,” Joi Harris, president and chief executive officer of DTE Energy, said in a statement. VPPs can smooth out demand peaks, reducing the utility’s need to invest in grid-infrastructure upgrades and generate kilowatt-hours with expensive fossil fuel peaker plants, both of which would pile costs on consumers. The initiative ​“should work well for the residents, too,” Hall said. ​“DTE will pay us a little bit to be part of this project.” Because the utility will pull battery power automatically when the grid is strained and electricity…

items.title: Model choice and prompt framing in LLM sustainability judgments
items.summary_raw: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for sustainability assessment and decision support, yet their judgments may depend on the selected model and on how the task is defined. We compare 13 locally executed open-weight LLMs on 80 author-written sustainability scenarios using three prompt families that ask which actor should be responsible, bear the costs, or initiate action. Each model answered at two temperature settings with 100 repetitions, producing 624,000 deposited outputs, of which 610,708 contain a complete score vector. Scores were analyzed as relative actor support after removing each response’s overall level. Within this instrument, the cost prompt family produced the highest cross-model disagreement, exceeding both responsibility and catalyst by 7.37 points (question-cluster 95% intervals 5.56−9.15 and 5.38−9.36, describing variation across these 80 scenarios). It also produced the most lead-actor disagreement and the lowest full consensus. Moving from catalyst to cost reduced relative support for government and increased it for individuals and firms; moving from cost to responsibility largely reversed this pattern. These differences exceeded temperature-setting differences and persisted under model exclusion, alternative score transformations and tie rules, missing-response checks, and stems without explicit cost wording. Exploratory category patterns are conditional on uneven item coverage. Secondary rationale-language comparisons show the same…

Greenhouse Farming: Cultivating the Future
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Greenhouse farming is widely promoted as a route to climate-resilient and resource-efficient food production, yet claims about its benefits are often repeated without clear baselines. This narrative review examines protected cultivation, with particular attention to India, covering structure types, automation and digital technologies, environmental and economic performance, policy support and socio-economic effects. Evidence was drawn from peer-reviewed studies, Indian farm-level economic analyses, official guidelines and recent survey data, and each quantitative claim is reported with its crop, location, comparison baseline and evidence type. About 14,400 ha of greenhouse structures were built in India between 2005 and 2020, over half of them low-technology, and expert estimates suggest that a large share is no longer operating. Water-use efficiency gains are well documented but shrink when the baseline is drip-irrigated field production or when evaporative cooling is needed. Recent Indian farm studies report higher yields and benefit–cost ratios above one for polyhouse vegetables, but with several-fold higher costs, and some crop–scale combinations are not viable. Greenhouse produce can have a higher carbon footprint per kilogram than open-field produce unless energy use is low or renewable. AI-based climate control has been demonstrated mainly in research-scale, high-technology compartments, and evidence on employment and women’s participation is thin. The paper concludes…

items.title: Rapid diffusion, widening inequality: Housing position and rooftop solar access in the Netherlands
items.summary_raw: Residential rooftop solar is expanding rapidly, but access remains uneven across households. This study examines how income inequality in rooftop solar access evolved during rapid diffusion in the Netherlands. It also examines the extent to which this inequality is associated with housing position, measured through tenure and dwelling type. Using Dutch Housing Survey data for 2018, 2021 and 2024, I analyse 127,701 household-dwelling observations, capturing both dwelling- and building-level solar access. Access increased across all income groups but much more strongly among higher-income households, widening the weighted gap between the highest and lowest income deciles to 44.8 percentage points by 2024. The adjusted 2024 income gap was roughly halved after housing characteristics were taken into account, although a substantial gap remained. The findings show that rooftop solar inequality is closely associated with housing position but is not reducible to it alone, highlighting the importance of considering housing-based barriers alongside financial constraints in equitable solar policy.

items.title: Relevance of traditional knowledge of food preservation for disaster preparedness and climate change adaptation in Pacific Islands: A case study from Nabuna Village, Koro Island

Traditional Knowledge (TK) provides locally grounded knowledge of environmental conditions, seasonal patterns, food preservation and weather observation, but its transmission and use are changing alongside sociocultural and technological developments. This study examines traditional food preservation, seasonal knowledge and weather forecasting in Nabuna Village, Koro Island, Fiji, with particular attention to their use and transmission across generations. A qualitative case study was conducted, informed by resilience theory and socio-ecological systems (SES) thinking. Data were collected through six age-and gender-stratified focus group discussions with 30 participants aged 18–89 years and analyzed thematically to examine food preservation practices, seasonal indicators, weather forecasting and intergenerational knowledge transmission. Participants described pit storage of root crops, drying and smoking of fish, and seasonal preservation and use of breadfruit and yams in relation to the Fijian traditional calendar ( Vula Vakaviti ) and environmental indicators. Older participants described using ecological cues, including changes in cloud patterns, wind direction, bird behavior and food availability, when anticipating weather conditions and preparing food and water. items.title: The Permitting Bill’s Next Battleground
items.summary_raw: On Thursday night, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a controversial bill that would revise federal environmental and energy laws to enable faster permitting of power lines, power plants, and other infrastructure. Now the bill heads to the House, where three questions will determine its fate: How many Republicans will show up to vote? What will Hakeem Jeffries do? And if it lands on Trump’s desk, what amendments will come with it? The current Speaker of the House, Republican Mike Johnson of Louisiana, said earlier this week that he would try to pass BAAJA under suspension, a process that would send it straight to the floor for a vote the week after Thanksgiving. But a successful suspension vote would require a two-thirds majority of however many lawmakers actually show up, and since the midterms, many Republicans who lost their seats have checked out. House leadership canceled several votes this week after too few showed up to hold the party line. If all House Republicans were present and voted in favor of the bill, it would still need some 71 Democrats to support it — and the amount of Democratic support, as we’ll discuss, is unclear. Johnson is trying to rally his party to show up, but if he can’t get them to come back, the bill would need even higher numbers on the Democrat side. House Democrats, meanwhile, are split. Some, like Representative Scott Peters of California, argue that while BAAJA isn’t perfect, it’s a good deal that’s…

items.title: The Freakout Over the Data Center Loophole That Wasn’t
items.summary_raw: Call it the data center loophole that wasn’t – and the beginning of a new kind of whiplash in energy and tech. For roughly 48 hours, many souls in Washington D.C. were quietly panicking that the Senate permitting bill’s strongest policy against data centers was about to be weakened. On Tuesday, senators released new changes to the manager’s amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act addressing issues holdouts on the bill raised about tribal consultation. Included in those modifications however was another change: Senators added language to the bill’s landmark ratepayer protection provision we’ve written about exempting new classes of facilities providing “Internet access” or “information services” as defined under two of the few federal tech statutes on the books. The apparent intention of this addition was to try and stop the new provisions from becoming a burden on small data centers involved in critical infrastructure, broadband and basic Internet services – the people making sure you have WiFi and cable. But critics of the bill said the specific language senators chose was potentially going much further than that. As written, the bill applied the ratepayer protection requirements to “computational load sites” which it defines as those that “primarily contain information technology infrastructure involved in” one of four activities: 1) “creating, executing, and delivering software applications and services,” 2) “artificial intelligence training,” 3)…

Like many of us in energy and environment professions, DeJarnett didn’t expect to be working on data centers, until she started being invited to communities fighting these projects to provide her perspective and public health expertise. She’s since become one of the go-to voices from the previous administration when it comes to data center conflicts and community relationships. I wanted to talk to Natasha about her time in the previous government and how it shapes her perspective on data centers. The following conversation was lightly edited for clarity. items.title: The microbial world of male reproduction
items.summary_raw: The last decade has brought renewed interest to microbial influences on host biology, yet the roles of microbes in host reproductive biology are underappreciated and often defined by a profound maternal bias. This perspective synthesizes emerging evidence across the tree of life to highlight the paternal microbiome as an overlooked driver of fitness, reproductive output, and intergenerational health, impacting epigenetic sculpting of the sperm and embryo, sexual transmission of microbes, and male gamete functions. These contributions indicate that mating can involve interactions between holobionts rather than simply the union of the maternal and paternal genomes. Thus, uniting male reproduction with the growing generalizations of microbial symbiosis guides several conceptual, theoretical, and empirical avenues for research in the life sciences.

items.summary_raw: Multi-principal element alloys are promising structural materials for nuclear, aerospace, and fusion applications, yet their accelerated discovery is limited by the prohibitive cost of evaluating point-defect transport and self-healing behavior across vast compositional spaces. Here, we establish local lattice distortion (LLD), an intrinsic feature of chemically complex alloys, as a predictive and universal descriptor for vacancy–interstitial diffusivity convergence. We develop and validate a high-fidelity machine-learning interatomic potential based on the moment tensor potential formalism for body-centered-cubic Zr–Ti–Nb alloys, enabling accurate large-scale simulations of defect energetics and migration. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal a robust inverse correlation between LLD and the activation energy disparity between vacancies and interstitials. This relationship is further validated in face-centered-cubic V–Co–Ni and Ni–Pd systems, demonstrating transferability across distinct chemistries and crystal structures. LLD-induced narrowing of vacancy–interstitial mobility differences promotes Frenkel pair recombination and defect self-healing. Mechanistically, vacancy diffusion is governed by the energy barrier associated with bond-length compression at the saddle state, together with statistical sampling of low-barrier jumps mediated by oversized atoms. These findings establish lattice distortion as a powerful, physically grounded design lever that links nanoscale…

A genome-wide senescence synthetic lethality screen identifies PARP16 as a senolytic target
items.summary_raw: Accumulation of senescent cells is increasingly viewed as a significant contributor to aging and age-related diseases. To date, the elimination of senescent cells through small molecule senolytic agents has largely relied on a limited number of repurposed agents, often leveraged from previous oncological applications. Here, we describe a CRISPR-based, genome-wide, synthetic lethal screen for senescent cells. From this screen, we identify a number of genes whose deletion appears to be well tolerated in normal proliferating cells, but whose deletion is lethal in the context of senescence. We further characterize one promising candidate gene encoding the ER-resident protein PARP16. Knockdown of PARP16 does not affect the viability of mouse or human cells but results in the death of a wide range of senescent cells. Furthermore, two distinct small molecule PARP16 inhibitors have little effect of normal cell growth but result in the selective death of senescent cells in culture and in freshly isolated human donor lung tissue explants. Together, these results demonstrate a rational strategy to identify novel senolytic therapies that could have potential applications for a wide range of age-related conditions.

items.title: Knowledge gaps and scientific progress
items.summary_raw: Knowledge production is often viewed as an endogenous process in which discovery arises through the recombination of existing theories, findings, and concepts. Yet not all recombinations are equally valuable, and identifying those that may prove most generative remains challenging. We propose that a crucial form of recombination occurs when linking concepts creates knowledge gaps—empty regions in the conceptual landscape that may focus scientific attention on unexplored connections. Using computational topology, we develop a method to identify knowledge gaps in science at scale. In this framework, gaps form when new connections complete cycles in evolving networks of scientific concepts. We apply the method to 34,363,623 papers in Microsoft Academic Graph spanning 1900 to 2020. The main analyses use samples ranging from 8,643,571 to 31,983,201 papers. Compared with papers that introduce novel concept pairs without opening gaps, gap-opening papers have greater long-term citation impact, are more disruptive of prior work, and exhibit greater delayed recognition. Gap-opening papers receive fewer citations within five years of publication but more over twenty years, consistent with scientific communities needing time to recognize and develop newly opened research territories. Evidence for the generative capacity of gap-opening papers—as indicated by high citation impact and disruption—replicates in five additional databases (OpenAlex, the PubMed Knowledge Graph, Dimensions…

items.title: A zero-one law for one-shot system identification
items.summary_raw: Can a model be identified from one experiment? We study analytic systems that are linearly parameterized by a combination of prescribed dictionary terms, such as partial differential operators and dynamical systems. For a single input-response pair, recovery is possible exactly when the evaluated dictionary terms are linearly independent. We prove a sharp zero-one law: either no input uniquely determines the coefficients, or almost every random input sampled from a nondegenerate Gaussian measure does. This dichotomy reduces one-shot system identification to a question about degenerate inputs and provides an a posteriori certificate in the noiseless setting. Numerical examples recover dynamical systems, nonlinear partial differential equations, and structured matrix families from single trajectory data, while also detecting when an extra probe is necessary.

Výsledky jejich studie tak naznačily, že počátky uspořádání lidského těla sahají daleko hlouběji do evoluční historie, než si odborníci doposud mysleli. Studie byla publikována ve vědeckém časopise Nature Communications. Akademie věd o tom v pátek informovala v tiskové zprávě.

items.title: Renne Dang: Za vulgární texty o ženách se nestydím. Nebyly etické, ale chtěli jsme provokovat

items.title: Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states
items.summary_raw: It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet translating “a lot” to real numbers pinned to individual facilities requires usage data, something that data-center operators are loath to disclose. A Harvard-led study published this week in Nature Sustainability gets us closer to these numbers. Researchers extracted locations and building footprints for as many U.S. hyperscale data centers as possible, ultimately cataloguing 403 of the warehouse-sized facilities across the country. Translating power capacity to theoretical electricity usage, the authors estimated these facilities gobble up roughly 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes. They suggest this electricity is associated with about 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions. The 82-TWh estimate corresponds to about 2 percent of U.S. electricity. Though noteworthy in its own right, that figure shrouds high state-to-state variability, with many states boasting data-center electricity shares in the double digits. When viewed as a fraction of the retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) in 2024, Oregon’s studied data centers used the equivalent of 18.6 percent of the electricity sold in the state. items.title: Is it OK to want a ‘normal life’ during the climate crisis?
items.summary_raw: “I would love to be a parent, but I worry it is unethical to bring children into a world that is wrecked by climate change.” “It feels kind of silly to be bothering with working a normal job and planning for retirement in some distant future, given the overall circumstances.” “Sometimes I feel hypocritical, working toward a better, more sustainable future while not fully reflecting those values in my own daily choices.” “My partner and I are thinking about buying our first home together and becoming parents. How can I make plans for the future in a world that is unravelling?” In the many questions we’ve received through the Ask a Climate Therapist form , I’ve noticed a theme running through several of them. People longing to have children, but grappling with the ethics of that decision. People wanting to enjoy occasional travel or an omnivorous diet, but feeling the sting of guilt. People hoping to plan for retirement or home ownership, but unsure how to reconcile those long-term visions with their fears and doubts about our climate future. I’d sum it up like this: Knowing what we know about the climate crisis, and knowing that we each must do our part to contribute to a liveable future, is it OK to want to enjoy life, too? items.title: A race at all costs? Economic and environmental effects of geoeconomic rivalry in clean energy technologies
items.summary_raw: Major economies are increasingly protecting their domestic clean-technology industries from one another. We ask what happens if this protection becomes reciprocal and escalates. Using regulatory, fiscal, or trade policies to protect and promote the interests of national industries against external competition may increase the cost of transformation and delay the diffusion of key low-carbon technologies. But how large are these effects? And do these measures actually help to achieve the objective of strengthening domestic industrial competitiveness and resilience of domestic industries? Employing a macroeconomic model, we assess scenarios with varying stringency of protectionism in which the five leading industrial economies symmetrically impose import tariffs on clean energy technologies and their upstream value chains and recycle the revenues into subsidies for domestic producers. We find that this reciprocal tariff escalation may double the mitigation cost for some regions in the most stringent case. Its environmental effects are small as reduced economic growth compensates for less efficient climate action. We also show that protective tariffs are hardly effective where major economies deploy them symmetrically. Only under the most stringent assumptions can we observe some limited success in boosting domestic competitiveness of green industries. Our analysis provides a first quantification of the economic and environmental costs of the geoeconomic turn in decarbonisation…

items.title: Linking sustainability knowledge, attitude, and commitment in university education
items.summary_raw: Non-Technical Summary Universities can help students understand sustainability and apply it in their decisions. We analysed 1,075 students from four Spanish universities. Greater sustainability knowledge was associated with more positive attitudes and stronger personal commitment. Knowledge was linked to students’ perceptions of sustainability’s business impact indirectly, through attitudes and commitment. These findings support teaching that brings together knowledge, values, and action. As the study captures one point in time, the relationships should not be interpreted as proof of cause and effect. Technical Summary We examine associations between sustainability knowledge, attitude, individual commitment, and perceived sustainability impacts on business performance among 1,075 students from four Spanish universities. We used partial least squares structural equation modelling with 10,000 bootstrap resamples to examine direct and indirect relationships. Knowledge was associated with attitude ( β ≈ 0.53) and commitment ( β ≈ 0.32), while attitude was associated with commitment ( β ≈ 0.32). Business-impact perceptions were associated with attitude ( β ≈ 0.53) and commitment ( β ≈ 0.15). The specified model linked knowledge to business-impact perceptions indirectly, primarily through attitude, with a weaker pathway through commitment. A direct path was not estimated. Reported model fit and reliability indices met the recommended thresholds. The findings extend…

items.title: Greenwashing and Climate Change Concerns in the Sustainable Development Agenda: Definition, Communication Strategies and Underlying Reasons
items.summary_raw: In the tourism and hospitality industry, greenwashing related to the climate is leading to deceptive environmental communication. Mass media play a critical role in providing information and shaping public opinions. Hence, this calls for accountability for greenwashing and its impact on climate change. This study examines 230 online news articles and 50 videos using Gioia's approach to present a multi‐dimensional examination of greenwashing in the tourism and hospitality industry. The data analysis revealed four aggregate dimensions: the meaning and concerns about greenwashing, the types of communication claims and the reasons for greenwashing, representing key themes of greenwashing conversations in popular media discourse related to the tourism and hospitality industry. Each dimension and its underlying constructs unfold the layers of greenwashing, which are exceedingly ambiguous. The study found that the media content presents different types of greenwashed claims. They range from absolute lies to misleading visual imagery. The findings of the study present an inherently contested, evolving and context‐dependent nature of the concept of greenwashing. The media discourse notably highlights ‘passing the buck’ as an important underlying reason for greenwashing in the tourism and hospitality industry.

items.title: Urban references and the visibility of energy supply and services in online climate discourse
items.source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.summary_raw: Energy transitions depend on both energy production and the services provided to users, yet their relative visibility in online climate discussion is poorly understood. We analyzed a keyword-bounded historical X/Twitter archive (January 2022–May 2023), identifying 62,009 energy-related posts within 786,101 cleaned records. Of these, 761 explicitly referred to cities or urban contexts. Supply/generation expressions occurred in 24.44% of urban-energy posts versus 33.41% of other energy posts (month-adjusted, author-clustered odds ratio [OR] 0.645; 95% CI 0.479–0.869). Demand/thermal-service expressions were directionally more frequent (OR 1.421; 95% CI 0.946–2.134), but the interval crossed parity. A restricted demand-only versus supply-only comparison showed a relative compositional difference (OR 1.919; 95% CI 1.220–3.018). These exploratory lexical associations raise a question for energy-policy communication about which energy-system functions become visible at different scales. They do not measure policy preferences, representative public opinion or causal framing effects.

items.title: Reparations in the context of the international climate funds: a climate justice comparison
items.summary_raw: With momentum for climate reparations continuing to grow, the newly established Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) is seen by some as an avenue for reparations in effect, if not in name. However, whether the FRLD constitutes a mechanism for climate reparations is not universally agreed. This article explores what a funding mechanism for climate reparations might entail in practice. To do this, I identify five qualities of a functional climate reparations fund: just governance; link between responsibility, sources of funding, and recipients; appropriate funding modality; appropriate and accessible delivery; and political feasibility and durability. I then compare these qualities to the experiences of climate funds already established under the UNFCCC’s Financial Mechanism to assess the extent to which they exhibit these qualities in practice, finding a consistent pattern of justice shortcomings across the funds. Although the FRLD falls short of reparative ideals, in broadening conceptualisations of the kinds of climate funds that are possible, its realisation nevertheless represents a significant milestone in the pursuit of climate justice.

items.title: Waste-to-Energy in Malaysia: Technologies, Biomass Resources, Municipal Solid Waste Management, Techno-Economic Feasibility, Environmental Impacts and Future Prospects
items.source_name: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
items.summary_raw: Waste-to-energy (WtE) technology has emerged as an important alternative for addressing the growing challenges of solid waste management while supporting the transition towards renewable and sustainable energy systems. In Malaysia, rapid urbanisation, population growth, industrial development and increasing consumption have contributed to rising municipal solid waste (MSW) generation, placing considerable pressure on existing landfill-based disposal systems. At the same time, Malaysia possesses substantial energy recovery potential from various waste streams, including food waste, agricultural residues, oil palm biomass, industrial waste and municipal solid waste. This paper presents a comprehensive review of waste-to-energy technologies, with particular emphasis on their suitability, performance, implementation challenges and future prospects in Malaysia. The review examines major WtE conversion pathways, including incineration, anaerobic digestion, landfill gas recovery, gasification, pyrolysis and hydrothermal carbonisation, together with emerging opportunities for biogas, biofuel and hydrogen production. Particular attention is given to the availability and characteristics of Malaysian waste feedstocks, especially organic municipal solid waste, food waste and oil palm residues. The paper further evaluates the technical, economic, environmental, institutional and social considerations influencing WtE implementation, including energy recovery efficiency, greenhouse gas…

items.title: Climate anxiety and pro-environmental behavior: Evidence from The Netherlands
items.summary_raw: This study investigates the association between climate anxiety and pro-environmental behavior, while accounting for general psychological functioning, resilience, loneliness, and demographic characteristics in Dutch population. Both linear and potential curvilinear associations were explored, given inconsistent findings in previous research. We hypothesized that climate anxiety would be positively associated with pro-environmental behavior and would explain unique variance beyond other factors. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 285 participants aged 18–85. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were performed to test the incremental contributions of climate anxiety (linear and quadratic terms), general psychological functioning (stress, depression, and anxiety), resilience, loneliness (social and emotional), and demographic characteristics (gender, age, and education) in pro-environmental behavior. The full model explained 44.1% of the variance in pro-environmental behavior. Climate anxiety was a strong and consistent factor, accounting for a substantial increase in explained variance (Δ R² = .371, p < .001). The association was linear rather than curvilinear. General psychological complaints, resilience, and loneliness did not explain additional variance once climate anxiety was included. Demographic variables such as gender and education, were initially associated with pro-environmental behavior but were no longer significant after accounting for climate…

items.title: Geography Teachers’ Perspectives on Teaching Climate Change Using GIS
Power struggles: Coping strategies and energy needs during long-duration power outages
items.summary_raw: Across the United States, outage risk and social vulnerability increasingly coincide, yet few studies have focused on the specific lived experiences and coping mechanisms of marginalized populations. From 2000 to 2021, Michigan ranked second nationwide for large, frequent weather-related power outages. We interview 49 households in Ann Arbor, Michigan's Bryant neighborhood to understand how they recall coping with long-duration outages (≥12 hours), and which energy services residents would prioritize during future long outages if limited backup power were available. By combining semi-structured interviews with household income and utility data (including energy use and cost), we find outage impacts are unevenly distributed, with low-income households, renters, and caregivers facing compounded vulnerabilities. Households adopt a range of adaptive strategies, from short-term coping (e.g., generator use, shifting appliance use) to longer-term preparations, highlighting the role of both individual agency and structural constraints. Our findings illustrate how long outages produce cascading energy insecurity and reveal that resilience is not solely determined by technical capacity but is shaped by intersecting social, economic, and housing vulnerabilities. We conceptualize outage decision-making as a dynamic process influenced by tenure status, caregiving responsibilities, and financial resources, extending existing frameworks of energy vulnerability and resilience. items.title: Honouring multiple ways of knowing: narrative evidence in climate-health planning
items.summary_raw: Climate change is reshaping where and how people live, intensifying disasters, slow-onset hazards, and patterns of displacement with profound consequences for public health. Conventional climate-health planning tools provide essential information but do not always capture the cultural, relational, and knowledge systems that shape how communities experience harm, adapt, and envision their futures. This Commentary argues that climate-health planning should recognise forms of knowledge that are often overlooked by technocratic approaches, including land-based knowledge, oral traditions, cultural memory, caregiving practices, social networks, and community-defined meanings of safety and resilience. Many of these practices are sustained through intangible cultural heritage, including storytelling, poetry, song, ritual, language, food traditions, and social ceremony. We argue that narrative evidence should be recognised as a valuable and legitimate component of climate-health evidence and incorporated alongside predominant approaches to climate assessment and planning. Situating this argument within epistemological pluralism, we propose that narrative forms can document lived experiences of hazards, exposure pathways, barriers to care, locally developed adaptation strategies, and the social and cultural implications of proposed interventions. Expanding what counts as evidence, however, requires more than inclusion. It also requires shared governance, ethical engagement…

items.title: Supplying metals needed for the energy transition: The value of creative reassembly as a conceptual lens
items.summary_raw: Demand for metals continues to increase rapidly due to global income and population growth and is expected to accelerate due to the metal requirements of the clean energy transition. However, the metal supply system, which operates at both a local and global scale, has an organizational structure that impedes its ability to satisfy this demand. Observed increases in the amount of metal supplied by the system have resulted from a variety of changes (or reassemblies) to the relationships between existing organizations and groups in the system. There are several types of possible reassemblies, but only a few are common. Policies are needed to encourage or incentivize more of such reassembly activity. If reassembly were more common, metal supply systems would be more visible and accessible, leading to greater societal awareness of their importance. Non-traditional participation in the system would become a viable but unexplored alternative.

items.title: Public support for AI environmental policies in Japan and South Korea-Inputs for adaptive governance
items.summary_raw: Artificial intelligence (AI) can contribute to environmental sustainability while causing environmental problems. From the perspective of adaptive governance, we ask what the governments of Japan and South Korea would have to learn from their publics at the initial stage of adaptation. Using a 2024 survey of 700 citizens in each country, we find public support for a firm-targeted subsidy and a tax, with the tax receiving more support in both countries. Support was associated with concern about climate change and AI, and with anticipated environmental effectiveness. Trust in government was associated with subsidy support in Japan; no other trust association survived sensitivity analysis. Anticipated negative economic impact was associated with stronger tax support, though on a different time horizon in each country. We argue that support reaches further toward coercive instruments than innovation-first governance assumes, and that learning from it would require institutionalized citizen inputs and information on policy effects.

items.title: Climate Change, Human Displacement and Mobility Governance in Cameroon: A Critical Review of Environmental Drivers, Vulnerability and Policy Responses
items.source_name: Journal of Geography Environment and Earth Science International
items.summary_raw: Cameroon combines a steep climatic gradient, from the Sudano-Sahelian plains of the Lake Chad Basin to the humid Atlantic littoral, with some of the largest and most protracted displacement crises in Central Africa. Floods, droughts, rain-triggered landslides, coastal erosion and urban inundation already move people within the country, yet these movements unfold alongside insurgency, separatist conflict and intercommunal violence that dominate humanitarian accounting. This critical narrative review examines how climate-related displacement and wider climate mobilities in Cameroon have been conceptualised, evidenced and governed, and evaluates the strength of the claims that link climate change to displacement in the country. Peer-reviewed literature, francophone scholarship and authoritative institutional documents published between 2009 and 2026 were identified through multidisciplinary open scholarly databases, a regional open archive, institutional repositories and citation chasing, and were appraised qualitatively for relevance, methodological transparency, analytical depth, credibility and governance contribution. The synthesis shows that hazard science for Cameroon has advanced considerably, particularly for extreme rainfall, urban flooding and coastal change, whereas mobility outcomes are seldom measured directly. Claims that climate change drives displacement around Lake Chad and in the Logone floodplain rest more on policy narratives than on demonstrated causal…

items.title: Maize-based cropping systems in India: dynamics, drivers, and pathways towards climate-resilient sustainable intensification
items.summary_raw: Maize (Zea mays L.) is emerging as one of the most significant cereals in India because of its growing importance in food, feed, fodder and industry. Maize-based cropping systems are evolving toward sustainable intensification at an increasing rate, driven largely by climate variability, resource limitations, technological advances, and shifts in market demand. In this review, the status, dynamics, and future prospects of maize cropping systems in India are summarized through a systematic literature review based on the PRISMA 2020 framework. The studies were selected for qualitative synthesis to include a total of 84 studies. This review examines the evolution of significant maize-based farming systems across various agro climatic regions of India, their impact on productivity, resource utilization efficiency, soil health and agricultural profitability. It also highlights the key drivers of cropping system change, including climate variability, soil and water constraints, improved hybrids, mechanization, policy support, and market demand. Recent developments in conservation agriculture, integrated nutrient management, precision agriculture, and climate smart agriculture are discussed for their potential to enhance resilience and sustainability. Despite substantial advances, constraints such as regional yield gaps, resource degradation, lack of labor, and limited market linkages persist. The review identifies certain research gaps and highlights the need for integrated…

CLIMATE CHANGE, THE GLOBAL ENERGY TRANSITION, AND STRATEGIC AND CRITICAL MINERALS: BRAZIL’S ROLE IN ADDRESSING THREE CHALLENGES FACING THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY IN THE 21ST CENTURY
items.summary_raw: Este trabalho aborda o papel do Brasil ante três desafios vividos pela comunidade internacional neste século XXI. Descreve as mudanças climáticas contemporâneas; caracteriza o processo de transição energética global; avalia a participação dos minerais estratégicos e críticos na transição energética; e, por fim, demonstra o papel do Brasil ante estes os desafios climático, energético e mineral neste século XXI. Esta pesquisa adotou uma abordagem qualitativa para analisar o quando o Brasil poderia projetar-se no concerto das nações e fomentar seu desenvolvimento nacional por alinhar simultaneamente vantagens competitivas no tocante às temáticas climática, energética e mineral. O procedimento utilizado foi a revisão da literatura e documental, que envolveu a consulta a fontes classificadas em quatro categorias: (1) as que descrevessem as mudanças climáticas contemporâneas; (2) fontes que caracterizassem o processo de transição energética global; (3) as que avaliassem a participação dos minerais estratégicos e críticos na transição energética; e (4) aquelas fontes que demonstrassem o papel do Brasil ante os três desafios assumidos pela comunidade internacional neste século XXI. Os estudos apontaram o quanto o Brasil teria condições de melhorar os campos econômico, tecnológico, energético e mineral além de ser um importante partícipe da transição energética no sistema internacional.

items.title: Residents' Awareness of Challenges and Attitudes towards Local-Level Safety
items.summary_raw: Objectives The aim of this article is to conceptualise the relationships between residents’ awareness of threats, safety perceptions, civic attitudes, social participation, and shared responsibility for local safety, as well as to identify the main factors shaping these relationships. Methods The article adopts a theoretical and conceptual approach based on a literature review and selected documents on local safety, social resilience, civic participation, and social capital. Particular attention is given to education, communication, trust, social ties, and local cooperation. Results The analysis indicates that residents’ awareness involves not only knowledge of threats but also the ability to recognise and interpret them and take actions that support individual and community safety. The analysis also shows that objective safety conditions may differ from subjective perceptions of safety. Based on these relationships, the study proposes a conceptual model linking threat awareness, safety perception, civic attitudes, social participation, shared responsibility, and social resilience. Conclusions Local safety should be understood as a result of interaction between public institutions, security services, and local communities. Residents should therefore be regarded not only as recipients of protective measures but also as potential co-creators of local safety. The proposed model provides a framework for future empirical research and for strengthening social competencies, trust…

items.title: Meta Life Cycle Assessment, Techno-Economic Analysis, and Risk Assessment of Carbon Mineralization Pathways to Inform Policy Frameworks
items.summary_raw: Carbon mineralization can reduce both point-source and legacy CO2 emissions while minimizing long-term risk, and it is essential, urgent, and disconnected. There is no holistic governing carbon mineralization policy in the US or EU, even though carbon capture is already factored into all major global climate models, with mineralization (converting CO2 into stable carbonates) representing a major subset. If mineralization is to bolster the suite of climate mitigation strategies, it is vital that academic guidance be provided to inform the currently underinformed policy direction. To address this, this study presents a meta life cycle and techno-economic analysis of carbon mineralization pathways from both academia and industry, normalizing independent techno-economic, life cycle, and risk assessment (Monte Carlo) results within the context of US and EU policy. Results demonstrate that in situ mineralization achieves the greatest life cycle GHG emission reductions at the lowest cost and is the only pathway capable of gigaton-scale emission reductions commensurate with climate goals. Enhanced rock weathering also consistently delivers net-negative GHG removal at relatively low costs, but ex situ pathways achieve lower GHG emission reductions at higher costs, where several proposed pathways are net-CO2 positive as CO2 emitted throughout the process (transportation, electricity use, and natural gas combustion) offsets CO2 sequestered. Risks of leakage, hazards, global capacity…

items.title: Can IO Endorsements Influence Public Attitudes on Issues with Direct Personal Consequences? Evidence from the IAEA’s Safety Verification of Japan’s Treated Water Release
items.summary_raw: International organizations (IOs) are often expected to shape public attitudes by providing credible policy information. Yet existing research focuses largely on foreign and security policy, leaving unclear whether IO endorsements influence attitudes on issues with direct personal consequences. This study addresses this question by examining the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) safety verification of Japan’s 2023 treated water discharge—an issue that affects people’s health and food consumption decisions yet requires specialized knowledge to evaluate. Conducting a survey experiment in South Korea, we find that, on average, the IAEA’s endorsement did not significantly reduce public concern about Japanese seafood safety or the marine environment. However, it had a notable effect among respondents who distrusted the government and viewed the IAEA favorably. These findings suggest that IO endorsements can shape public attitudes on issues with direct personal consequences when political distrust of domestic authorities is combined with trust in the IO.

items.title: Integration of LECA blocks and phase change materials in external walls: Life cycle assessment and cost analysis
Environmental and material implications of global climate mitigation pathways
items.summary_raw: Reaching the goals of the Paris Agreement requires a rapid transformation of global energy systems. Yet, energy supply and use exert multiple pressures on ecosystems, human health and natural resources, raising questions about the broader environmental consequences of alternative decarbonization pathways and the resources they require. Here we analyse 24 climate mitigation pathways from three integrated assessment models using a life-cycle perspective. This enables a system-wide comparison of environmental impacts and resource requirements of global final energy provision from 2020 to 2100. We find that deep decarbonization delivers substantial cobenefits for human health and ecosystem quality, but does not systematically reduce pressures on land, water or mineral resource extraction. For metals central to electrification, climate change mitigation ambition primarily reshapes the timing of extraction rather than cumulative volumes. Pathways achieving similar climate targets can impose markedly different environmental and resource pressures, shaping the feasibility and desirability of alternative transitions.

items.title: Re-examining the relationship between artificial intelligence development and urban per capita carbon emissions within a government–market–public framework
items.summary_raw: Artificial intelligence (AI) development may be associated with urban emissions through technological applications and interactions among government, market, and public actors, yet city-level evidence remains limited. This study develops a government–market–public (GMP) framework using panel data for 279 Chinese cities from 2013 to 2021. A city-level AI development index combines government policy support, AI-related firms and patents, and public attention. Two-way fixed-effects models with city-clustered standard errors assess its association with urban per capita carbon emissions, supplemented by sensitivity, spatial, pathway-consistency, and heterogeneity analyses. AI development is negatively associated with urban per capita carbon emissions in the baseline model and under alternative controls, lagged controls, province-by-year fixed effects, most leave-one-out tests, and the spatial model. The relationship is not sustained with city-specific linear trends or first differences, and a significant lead term complicates its temporal interpretation. Spatial estimates show a significant local association but no significant cross-city spillover. GMP regressions yield exploratory patterns involving government intervention, population agglomeration, and household income rather than verified transmission processes. Interaction tests indicate stronger negative associations in coastal cities and provincial capitals or centrally administered municipalities; city-size results remain…

items.title: Networked agroecology as a pathway for climate change adaptation in Uganda
items.summary_raw: Agroecology is increasingly recognised as a pathway for strengthening climate change adaptation in smallholder farming systems, yet little research has examined how agroecological innovations are organised and sustained through inter-organisational networks in African contexts. This study examines how 25 member organisations of the Participatory Ecological Land Use Management Uganda (PELUM Uganda) network mobilise agroecological initiatives to support climate adaptation among farming communities in 17 districts. Using a qualitative case study design, we collected data from 194 participants (47% women), comprising member organisation staff and farmer group leaders, through 26 focus group discussions, six small-group interviews and 11 in-depth interviews, with document review, and analysed the data using codebook thematic analysis. Participants reported that member organisations promote seed conservation, soil and water conservation, renewable energy, market access, community collaboration and faith-based stewardship, and perceived these practices as contributing to climate adaptation. Participants identified limited government support, conflicting extension messages, short-term funding, limited local research, and weak market incentives as barriers and described farmer savings groups, a consortium arrangement, and proposals for joint fundraising as responses to fragmented donor funding. From this evidence, we propose “networked agroecology” as a meso-level lens that…

items.title: Determinants of Green Purchase Intention and Green Purchase Behavior Among College Students in Fujian, China
items.summary_raw: Purpose: This study addresses the limited evidence on factors influencing green purchase intention and green purchase behavior among college students in a regional vocational education context in China. Research design, data and methodology: A quantitative survey was conducted among 500 students from the Department of Automation Engineering at Meizhouwan Vocational Technology College. A non-probability sampling approach combining purposive, quota, and convenience sampling was adopted. A pilot test involving 30 participants was conducted, and content validity and reliability were assessed using the Item Objective Congruence method and Cronbach’s alpha. Confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling using AMOS were employed to evaluate the measurement model and test the hypothesized relationships. Results: Perceived behavioral control, subjective norms, attitude, environmental concern, and environmental knowledge significantly influenced green purchase intention (p < .05). Perceived behavioral control showed the strongest effect (β = 0.577), followed by subjective norms (β = 0.369). Green purchase intention significantly predicted green purchase behavior (β = 0.516). Conclusions: The findings demonstrate the importance of perceived behavioral control, social influence, and environmental awareness in strengthening green purchase intention, which subsequently promotes green purchase behavior. items.source_name: International Journal of Scientific Research in Science and Technology
items.summary_raw: Growing pressure on natural resources, climate change and increasing waste generation have created a need to move from the traditional linear economy towards more sustainable and circular production systems.Biobased products, including materials, chemicals, biofuels and energy, can be produced from renewable biomass, agricultural residues, industrial byproducts and waste streams, and when these resources are efficiently utilized and reused they can support a circular bio economy (CBE).Integrating bio economy and circular economy (CE) principles encourages efficient resource use, waste reduction, reuse and recycling, and the conversion of waste into valuable products.Bio-based materials such as bio plastics and bio-composites have considerable potential to reduce environmental impacts; however, competition with food production, landuse impacts, higher costs, feedstock variability and limited end-of-life management must be carefully considered, and bio refinery approaches can further support this transition by recovering useful chemicals, fuels and materials from industrial waste and effluents.Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is an important tool for understanding the environmental impacts of bio-based products throughout their life cycle, and combining it with Life Cycle Costing (LCC) and social Life Cycle Assessment (S-LCA) gives a broader view of environmental, economic and social sustainability.Valuechain mapping and circularity assessment can further help identify resource…

items.title: Scrolling through the storm: how compulsive digital habits reshape ecological grief
items.summary_raw: Ecological grief is grief for the loss of species, ecosystems, landscapes, and places. Solastalgia is a similar type of distress that occurs when unwanted change occurs in the environment of a person’s home. These ideas were initially intended to capture place-based experiences, but ecological distress is increasingly becoming digital media-mediated. Individuals are now flooded with continuous streams of information, such as climate-related disasters, loss of biodiversity, headlines, personal stories, images, and algorithmically selected content. This perspective suggests that doomscrolling goes beyond being just a symptom of greater recognition of ecological crises. Over time, compulsive digital behavior can change how people feel and express ecological grief through their emotions and behaviors. Distress or discomfort with the digital environment should not be mistaken for real-world loss. Despite this, over time digital exposure may increase climate anxiety and sense of powerlessness, add to symptoms of vicarious trauma, and displace restorative activities like sleep, social connection, and nature contact. Presently, there is no definitive evidence to conclude that social media plays an independent role in climate anxiety, as the available evidence remains mostly cross-sectional. Digital media may also support environmental learning, collective action, peer support, and conservation engagement. I thus suggest a differentiated framework of three inter-related pathways…

items.title: Message Framing Strategies in Sustainability Communication: An Analysis in Türkiye
items.summary_raw: Sustainability communication has become a strategic priority for organizations demonstrating their environmental, social, and economic commitments, and social media makes audience reactions observable. This study asks whether the framing characteristics of corporate sustainability messages affect consumer engagement in Türkiye. A total of 166 sustainability-related Instagram posts published in 2025 by companies in the BIST Sustainability 25 Index were content-analyzed across five framing variables; gain/loss framing, message direction, tonality, emotional appeal, and temporal focus, and engagement was measured through likes, comments, and shares. Three hypotheses were tested with independent samples t-tests on log-transformed engagement. Only temporal focus was significant: present-focused messages attracted higher engagement than future-focused ones, whereas tonality and emotional appeal did not. The immediacy of a message, rather than its tone, appears to drive engagement.

items.title: An Integrated Text Mining and Content Analysis to Inform Climate‐Smart Cocoa Practices
items.source_name: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
items.summary_raw: Climate‐smart cocoa practices are being championed as a strategy for addressing climate‐related risks in cocoa production systems. Despite growing recognition, adoption remains uneven due to structural, contextual, and knowledge‐related constraints. This study integrates evidence from two sources: a systematic review of 60 empirical studies and the first round of a modified Delphi study completed by 14 experts from four cocoa‐producing countries. Text mining of the recommendations extracted from these studies (124 statements consolidated into 60 study‐level documents) identified exploratory themes related to economic resilience, sustainable farming practices and capacity building, climate adaptation and extension services, and agroforestry. A complementary content analysis of the experts' open‐ended responses (54 responses received of a possible 154) revealed nuanced perspectives on the urgency of adoption, local understandings of climate change, implementation challenges, resistance to change, and the role of institutional networks. While both sources converged on the importance of strengthening extension systems and economic support, experts placed greater emphasis on locally grounded experiential knowledge, which was less visible in the literature. Lexical polarity of the literature‐derived recommendations was predominantly neutral or positive and did not differ by topic or by the country of the source study. The findings demonstrate the value of integrating computational…

items.title: Who is highly distressed and impaired by climate change? Cross-national cut-scores and a brief screener for population research
Operationalizing climate action and policy in U. S. healthcare
items.summary_raw: Global temperatures and greenhouse gas emissions continue to reach record highs, exacerbating climate change and its impacts on public health. Health care accounts for 5% of global emissions, and many health care systems are working to reduce their climate impact. Within the United States, numerous professional societies advocate for climate action, but operationalization remains inconsistent. U. S. healthcare lags behind international peers in mandating decarbonization and integrating climate health into medical education. To truly transform the U. S. health care system, healthcare entities must transition from voluntary pledges to an integrative policy framework that prioritizes sustainable procurement, fossil fuel divestment, and mandatory accreditation standards to ensure systemic resilience and protect public health.

items.title: Voters uncovered: home insurance and the electoral effects of climate costs
items.source_name: Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy
items.summary_raw: How do voters react to the financial costs of climate change? I study this question in the context of the growing home insurance crisis in the United States. Drawing on county- and ZIP code-level panel data, I examine whether home insurance distress has affected turnout and voter choices in gubernatorial and insurance commissioner elections in the period 2014–2024. I find that home insurance distress is associated with higher turnout and lower roll-off in downballot insurance commissioner races. By contrast, impacts on electoral returns across offices vary and do not provide consistent evidence for partisan or anti-incumbent effects. I interpret these results as indicating that home insurance distress is mobilizing voters, but in the absence of clear partisan issue ownership and messaging from incumbents, not yet systematically affecting their choices. Nevertheless, voter reactions to insurance distress may create incentives for incumbents to protect their constituents from climate costs, posing political risk – but also potentially providing leverage – to private insurers.

items.title: European Green Deal and climate change regulations: The Bulgarian perspective
items.summary_raw: Type of the article: Research ArticleAbstractThis study aims to map the legal framework and critically evaluate the transposition of EU regulations concerning climate change mitigation and the green energy transition in Bulgaria. It focuses on the institutional implementation deficits against the relevant European Green Deal legal benchmarks. The methodological approach incorporates both contemporary legal research methods and interdisciplinary analytical tools. The paper draws primarily on European policies for sustainable development, EU primary law, enacted climate change directives and regulations, and scholarly literature and research reports on relevant themes. The green transition in Bulgaria involves not simply the transposition of EU directives but the production of an autonomous national legal architecture having the formal capacity and legal credibility to drive the transformation from within. While Bulgaria has gradually aligned its national legislation with EU climate and energy law, the legislative action has been reactive and inefficiently attached to a coherent national vision of the energy sector. Transposition steps often occurred under direct pressure from the European Commission's infringement proceedings and financial sanctions imposed by the Court of Justice of the European Union. Based on its findings, the paper outlines recommendations for strengthening Bulgarian legal architecture in conformity with its obligations under the European Green Deal…

items.title: Meta Joins the Clean Materials Race
items.summary_raw: Meta is reconsidering its biggest climate promise. In its 2026 sustainability report , released Thursday afternoon, the company said it is “re-evaluating” its goal of reaching net-zero by 2030, amidst a 45% year-over-year increase in its emissions. That tracks with the broader skepticism toward Meta’s climate bonafides. When Heatmap asked a group of our sharpest energy insiders late last year which hyperscaler they thought was doing the best on climate , Google and Microsoft emerged as clear frontrunners, while Meta narrowly beat out Amazon in the race to the bottom. It was not surprising. After all, Google pioneered the concept of 24/7 energy matching , and made early bets on advanced geothermal and small modular reactors . Microsoft built the carbon removal market practically singlehandedly while making deals with low-carbon materials suppliers like steelmaker Stegra and clean cement startup Sublime Systems. Meta, meanwhile, was making headlines for its gigantic new data center campus in Louisiana, which it aims to power with 7.5 gigawatts of new natural gas plants. This summer, it also quit RE100, a pledge to power operations with 100% renewable electricity. A spokesperson for the Climate Group, the nonprofit that runs the program, said Meta had to withdraw “as it is no longer able to meet the technical criteria due to investments made in new gas power.” Microsoft and Google are still parties to the pledge, and have kept their respective 2030 targets in place — though…
