items.title: Cryo-EM provides insight into how the Staphylococcus aureus IsdH receptor removes hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin complex
items.summary_raw: Staphylococcus aureus extracts hemin from human hemoglobin (Hb) to overcome host-imposed iron limitation. How it recovers Hb-bound hemin from the hemoglobin:haptoglobin (Hb:Hp) complex, the major circulating form of Hb outside red blood cells, remains unclear. Here, we use cryo-electron microscopy, biophysical measurements, and solution kinetics to define how the S. aureus IsdH surface receptor extracts hemin from Hb:Hp. A 3.1 Å cryo-EM structure of Hb:Hp bound by full-length IsdH reveals that its N-terminal NEAT domain (N1) anchors it to αHb, whereas its downstream N2N3 extraction unit engages βHb to remove its hemin. The receptor engages Hb:Hp differently than isolated Hb, because N-linked glycans on haptoglobin bias the extraction unit toward βHb, sterically occluding its access to αHb while still permitting engagement by N1. Kinetic assays show that IsdH actively accelerates hemin release from Hb:Hp. Three-dimensional variability analysis indicates that this likely occurs via a dynamic interface in which receptor motions reposition the extraction unit relative to βHb, collectively supporting a model in which IsdH transiently perturbs the F-helix to promote hemin extraction. Alignment of that model with a previously determined CD163:Hb:Hp structure shows how IsdH may disrupt Hb:Hp recognition by macrophage and monocyte CD163 receptors, helping to explain how it may hinder clearance of Hb:Hp from circulation. In aggregate, these results help define the structural basis for…

items.title: Co-translational surveillance of nascent polypeptides times circadian rhythms in Drosophila
items.summary_raw: Ribosome-associated quality control (RQC) ensures proteostasis by actively degrading aberrant translation intermediates on stalled ribosomes, yet its physiological role in gene regulation remains elusive. Here, we demonstrate that Drosophila circadian clocks employ RQC to sustain 24-h behavioral rhythms. RNA interference-mediated depletion of RQC components in circadian pacemaker neurons impaired free-running locomotor rhythms. In particular, the loss of Caliban ( Clbn ) function in clearing 60S-associated faulty polypeptides led to weak but long-period rhythms in adult locomotor activity. These behavioral phenotypes were accompanied by delayed accumulation of the core clock protein PERIOD (PER), most evidently in pigment-dispersing factor-expressing clock neurons, and dampened structural plasticity of their axons. per heterozygosity exaggerated CLBN depletion-induced period lengthening, whereas overexpression of the PER-associating factor TIMELESS blunted this effect. Clbn deficiency in Drosophila S2R+ cell cultures increased the generation of prematurely terminated PER species, particularly when PER translation is high, and sensitized full-length PER to phosphorylation-dependent decay. These findings support PER as a clock-relevant RQC substrate, providing a mechanistic link between translation flux, co-translational surveillance, and circadian timekeeping.

items.title: Morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment
items.summary_raw: Modern western legal and criminal justice theories assume that punishment should deter criminalized behavior by introducing costs that reduce its expected utility, but, empirically, punishment often has weak effects on rates of crime and recidivism. Here, we hypothesize that when people are motivated to engage in criminalized behavior for moral reasons, they show diminished sensitivity to punishment. We demonstrate our hypothesis across 10 correlational, experimental, and economic game studies with participants drawn from the general population as well as participants with criminal backgrounds. Studies 1 to 3 draw on federal data of over 30,000 offenders and find that participants’ estimates of moral motives for crime predict higher recidivism while estimates of material motives predict the opposite. Studies 4 to 8 use judgment studies and find that morally motivated crimes are less sensitive to punishment across a diversity of crime types, when motives are manipulated but actions are kept constant, persist for different types of consequences, and are unique to moral motivation. Studies 9 and 10 employ economic games and find that when players take money from others for moral reasons, they are less deterred by the imposition of fines. Implications for systems of punishment, offender psychology, and restorative justice approaches are discussed.

items.title: Causal dynamic resonance reduces false positives in detecting causality
items.summary_raw: Many dynamical systems in nature, such as brains and weather systems, are highly nonlinear and complex. Determining information flow among the components that make up these dynamical systems is challenging. If the components are the result of a common process or become synchronized, causality measures typically fail. We previously introduced Cross-Dynamical Delay Differential Analysis, a nonlinear method for assessing causal influence, along with a complementary approach for dynamical similarity between time series data, Dynamical Ergodicity Delay Differential Analysis. Here, we show that “Causal Dynamic Resonance (CDR)” further improves the false positive rejection rate by adding white noise to the data, without perturbing the underlying dynamical system. This is followed by a study of CDR in coupled Rössler systems, where ground truth interactions are known and in invasive intracranial electroencephalographic data from drug-resistant epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring.

items.title: Counterions, polarization, and pore hydration relay drive ion permeation through hydrophobic pore formed by the MERS coronavirus E protein
items.summary_raw: Hydrophobic pores are generally expected to exclude ions because the large desolvation penalty associated with ion transfer cannot be compensated within a nonpolar environment. The envelope (E) protein of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) presents a striking exception, conducting cations with high efficiency despite forming a predominantly hydrophobic pore. To resolve this apparent paradox, we combine finite-temperature string simulations with additive and polarizable force fields to determine the minimum free-energy pathways for ion permeation through the MERS E channel. The simulations reveal a cooperative permeation mechanism in which transient counterion association, localized pore hydration, and electronic polarization jointly reduce the desolvation penalty. Rather than acting as passive spectators, counterions transiently chaperone the permeating cation before dissociating within the channel, thereby lowering the energetic cost of charge desolvation while preserving net ionic conductance. Explicit electronic polarization further reshapes the pore hydration landscape and cation– π interactions, leading to substantially reduced free-energy barriers and a permeation mechanism that is in substantially better agreement with experiment. These results suggest that efficient ion transport through hydrophobic pores arises from the cooperative interplay between electrostatics, polarization, and hydration rather than complete pore wetting, providing both a…

items.title: Lactate-rich tumor employs the KAT5–HIF1α axis to modulate the activity of the hypoxia pathway and facilitates tumor progression
items.summary_raw: Substantial evidence shows that hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) up-regulates glycolytic enzymes and promotes lactate production, which contributes to “Warburg Effect.” Nevertheless, the impact of lactate or lactylation modification on hypoxia signaling pathways within the tumor microenvironment remains largely unclear. Here, we report that lactate can induce the upregulation of hypoxia pathway activity in a HIF1α-dependent manner. We identified that KAT5 as a lysine lactyltransferase of HIF1α and the “writer” responsible for lactylation at HIF1α K389, K460, K674, and K682, and HDAC2 as a HIF1α de-lactylase. The lactylation-deficient mutant of HIF1α (HIF1α 4KR ) reduced HIF1α stability, along with down-regulating hypoxia-mediated angiogenesis, metastasis, apoptosis, and glycolysis. Mechanistically, the HIF1α 4KR mutant enhances the binding of HIF1α to von Hippel-Lindau tumor suppressor protein (VHL), facilitating its degradation. MG149, a KAT5 inhibitor, can enhance the efficacy of anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)-based combination immunotherapy in a murine model by suppressing hypoxia pathway activity in tumor cells and potentiating the cytotoxic function of CD8 + T cells. Clinically, lactylated HIF1α and KAT5 are up-regulated in breast cancer tissues compared with adjacent tissues. Notably, elevated levels of HIF1α lactylation and KAT5 expression were observed in resistant cancer specimens from triple-negative breast cancer patients who had undergone…

items.title: Serine–glycine lipid homeostasis in Bacteroidota modulates membrane stability and host interactions
items.summary_raw: Lipid 1256 (L1256) is a large complex aminolipid produced by members of the phylum Bacteroidota that is formed by addition of a phosphatidic acid (PA) moiety to the precursor aminolipid, L654. Studies have shown that L1256 is enriched in diseased gingival tissues, linking synthesis of this aminolipid to sites of chronic inflammation. Given that PA is involved in membrane rearrangements and L654 is a known Toll-like receptor 2 ligand associated with health, we hypothesized that synthesis of L1256 could influence outer membrane vesicle (OMV) biogenesis and innate immune responses. Here, PG1647 was identified as a lipid synthase required for biosynthesis of L1256 in Porphyromonas gingivalis . Loss of PG1647 abolished L1256 and related minor species, while impairing membrane stress resistance and intracellular survival. PG1647 loss also increased OMV production and enhanced the proinflammatory activity of bacterial cells and OMVs. These phenotypes occurred without broad transcriptional changes, supporting lipid remodeling as a central driver. Structural and biochemical analyses supported a phospholipase D-like role for PG1647. Complementation with the Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron homologue BT3978 restored L1256 production in P. gingivalis and partially rescued associated phenotypes, suggesting functional conservation among the host-associated Bacteroidota . Additional studies determined that many species in the phylum Bacteroidota carry a similar functional enzyme, further…

items.title: Coevolving gene networks underlying a phenotypic syndrome revealed via integrating comparative genomic and microevolutionary analyses
items.summary_raw: Complex adaptive traits often comprise interacting, coevolving phenotypes that together for a syndrome that is shaped by multiple genetic loci. While using intraspecific variation is an established approach for investigating syndromes, such polymorphism typically captures only a subset of syndrome traits. Diapause, an alternative developmental pathway that evolved independently in many species to synchronize life cycles with resource availability, exemplifies this challenge. While subsets of this essential phenotype have long been studied at a single species level, the genomic basis of the full diapause syndrome remains poorly understood. This paucity of insights has fueled a long-standing debate about how life cycle synchronization evolves and whether convergent phenotypes employ shared mechanisms. Using a comparative genomic analysis spanning diverse diapause transitions in butterflies, we identified a large network of coevolving genes unique to diapausing species. The network is composed of functional modules spanning circadian regulation, metabolism, and cell cycle control. We tested whether this macroevolutionary scale network predicts microevolutionary dynamics, hypothesizing that this network is the polygenic architecture underlying the diapause syndrome. Analyses revealed that allelic variation in the diapause network is significantly enriched in signatures of local adaptation across latitudes, but only in diapausing species. Thus, we empirically show that diapause…

items.title: Preemptive solving of future problems: Multitask Preplay in humans and machines
items.summary_raw: Humans can pursue a near-infinite variety of tasks, but typically can only pursue a small number at the same time. We hypothesize that humans leverage experience on one task to preemptively learn solutions to other tasks that were accessible but not pursued. We formalize this idea as “Multitask Preplay”, an algorithm that replays experience on one task as the starting point for “preplay”—counterfactual simulation of an accessible but unpursued task. Preplay is used to learn a predictive representation that can support fast, adaptive task performance later on. When implemented within deep reinforcement learning, it predicts human generalization to novel tasks more accurately than traditional planning and predictive representation methods across grid-worlds and a 2D Minecraft domain. Additionally, Multitask Preplay improves an artificial agent’s ability to generalize to new environments sharing task co-occurrence structure. These findings demonstrate that Multitask Preplay is a scalable theory of human counterfactual learning and generalization; endowing artificial agents with this capacity can significantly improve their performance in challenging multitask environments.

items.title: Physicochemical microenvironments within biomolecular condensates govern reaction kinetics beyond mass-action effects
items.summary_raw: Cells utilize phase separation to compartmentalize biochemical reactions within biomolecular condensates. Although these compartments can enhance reaction rates by concentrating reactants, how they modulate kinetics beyond mass-action effects remains poorly understood. Here, using spontaneous protein ligation as a model reaction, we examined how the physicochemical microenvironment within condensates modulates reaction kinetics. We systematically analyzed condensates formed by folded PRM–SH3 scaffolds and intrinsically disordered proteins (LAF, TAF, and FUS). We designed a proximity-sensitive client probe to assess excluded-volume-driven increases in effective reactant concentration. In parallel, we characterized condensate hydrophilicity and associated changes in water activity, identifying these properties as additional key kinetic determinants. Together, our findings elucidate how effective concentration and hydrophilicity jointly regulate biochemical reactions within condensates.

items.title: Lipid-induced Caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking is associated with lipid droplet growth
items.summary_raw: Caveolae are 50 to 100 nm sized plasma membrane invaginations involved in cellular lipid uptake and lipid accumulation. Several caveolin1 and cavin1 mutations are associated with human lipodystrophy. Previous research identified caveolae proteins at lipid droplets, although their specific cellular function at lipid droplets is not understood. Here, we show that extracellular dietary lipids like oleic acid and cholesterol shift caveolae at the plasma membrane to highly spherical invaginations and induce the internalization of caveolin1. Within 3 h of lipid treatment, caveolin1 accumulates specifically to lipid droplets. Correlative fluorescence Focused Ion Beam – Scanning Electron Microscopy and split-APEX proteomics revealed that this localization occurs in the absence of intact caveolar vesicles but caveolin1 alone. Mechanistically, caveolin1 trafficking to lipid droplets is regulated by EHD2 at the plasma membrane, is dynamin independent, and proceeds via EEA1- and Rab5-positive endosomes within 1 h of oleic acid treatment. Lipid droplet accumulation of caveolin1 is independent of lysosomal activity. Functionally, caveolin1-enriched lipid droplets exhibit a significant increase in size, demonstrating that caveolin1 is critical for lipid droplet growth. Notably, the deletion of the central caveolin1 β-barrel (Cav1-F160X), a mutation identified in lipodystrophy patients, abolished caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking and lipid droplet growth. Taken together, our results show…

items.title: Authentic structure of the CCHFV RNA–nucleoprotein complex at near-atomic resolution
items.summary_raw: Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) poses a major public health threat without approved vaccines or antivirals. Its ribonucleoprotein (RNP) is essential for replication, but its native architecture and RNA packaging remain elusive. Here, we combine AI-based structural prediction with cryo–electron microscopy to resolve the native structure of the CCHFV RNP purified from CCHFV-infected cells. We report a 3.87 Å structure of a single-turn RNP, and local refinement yielded a 3.55 Å structure of two adjacent NP protomers with continuous RNA. This represents the highest-resolution authentic RNP structure reported among segmented negative-strand RNA viruses (sNSVs), and provides the structural basis for CCHFV RNP assembly. Together with mutational analyses, these findings define the molecular basis of RNA encapsidation and NP oligomerization in the native CCHFV RNP. Our findings provide a hybrid structural framework integrating AI and experimental approaches for understanding genome organization in sNSVs and offer a foundation for future antiviral development.

items.title: Communicating heat risk: the psychological impact of naming and ranking heatwaves on threat perception & protective behavior
items.summary_raw: Abstract Extreme heat has emerged as the most lethal weather-related threat globally, yet warning systems often fail to motivate protective behavior, creating a critical gap in climate adaptation policy. Guided by the Extended Parallel Process Model, this study experimentally tests whether two communication cues borrowed from other hazard domains, personalized naming and categorical ranking, enhance public threat perception and protective intentions. A 2 × 2 randomized survey experiment ( N = 1,047) was conducted with a U.S. online sample, manipulating the presence of each cue in a standardized heatwave warning. Single-item Likert scales administered immediately after exposure measured the model’s three threat appraisal components (Perceived Severity, Perceived Vulnerability, and Fear) and Protective Behavioral Intentions. Linear regression models assessed main and moderation effects, controlling for demographic and climate belief covariates. Categorical ranking significantly increased all three components of threat appraisal. Naming had no measurable effect. Combining both cues was less effective than categorical ranking alone, suggesting a cognitive interference effect that may undermine complex messaging. The analyses also identified heterogeneity in how threat appraisal translates into protective intentions: men responded more strongly to fear and women to perceived vulnerability, while political affiliation moderated responses to perceived severity. These findings…

items.title: Even the ‘good guys’ of AI are locking in fossil fuels
items.summary_raw: Anthropic became one of the most valuable companies on the planet on Wednesday, valued at $1.5 trillion after its IPO. Known as one of the “good guys” of AI , Anthropic was founded by employees who left OpenAI over disagreements about ethics and safety. But despite the company’s emphasis on responsibility and preventing AI from killing everybody, one thing you don’t hear Anthropic talking about much is its contribution to climate change. Ahead of the initial public offering this week, Greenpeace accused the company of “asking average investors to join them in throwing the planet into the climate furnace.” AI data centers are causing electricity demand to soar and fueling a surge in natural gas plants . A recent report found that the biggest data centers in the United States emit about as much carbon dioxide as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark. Anthropic is contributing to that: It reportedly signed a $3.4 billion deal with the Texas-based company OnePWR Solutions in September to power data centers with gas-fired engines — the largest known single purchase of its kind by an AI lab. “It signals what direction they’re taking very clearly,” said Charlie Cray, a senior strategist at Greenpeace USA. The company is locking in fossil fuels at a time when scientists say the world is certain to overshoot the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees C . Anthropic’s reputation for being the most responsible of the AI giants means it should be minimizing its climate impact…

items.title: As black lung disease surges, the Trump administration proposes ‘deregulatory’ protections for miners
items.summary_raw: Coal mining is dangerous and takes a toll on the body, but a miner working underground can earn enough to buy a house, drive a nice car, and send the kids to college. There was a time when John Robinson thought the trade-off was worth it. No longer. He was diagnosed with black lung disease at age 47, a consequence of inhaling toxic silica dust in the mines of Virginia. “These companies will bait you in with this big money,” said Robinson, who is now 60 and vice president of the National Black Lung Association. “When you get down and out, well, guess what? You’re like an old wore-out tire on the car or something. items.summary_raw: This is Heatmap Daily, a weekday digest written by our executive editor. Subscribe here. The Senate will vote tonight on amendments to the permitting reform bill, officially known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. It will then vote on the bill itself — which only needs a bare majority to pass. The House of Representatives will then take up the bill . The permitting bill, in other words, appears to have survived that peculiar phase of Senate process where legislation requires 60 votes to pass. (That magic number isn’t due to anything in the Constitution, but because Senate procedure technically allows unlimited and silent “debate” on a measure, and it takes a three-fifths majority to end that “debate.” Changing this is what people mean when they talk about “ending the filibuster.”) All of this is to say that the bill’s Senate coalition might be as large now as it has ever been. Senators have now taken a handful of these 60-vote-threshold cloture votes on BAAJA, and we can see who voted for the measure last week at the beginning of the debate and who had peeled off by the end. As we await final votes on the amendments and the bill itself, here’s some brief game-time analysis: Almost every Republican voted yes. items.title: Follow the gas: State energy planning and heterogeneous liquefied petroleum gas infrastructure development in Indonesia's new capital frontier
items.summary_raw: This paper examines the planning and use of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) infrastructure in the frontier of Indonesia's new capital city, Ibu Kota Nusantara (IKN), East Kalimantan. The government envisions IKN as a green city using 100% renewable energy by 2045. Until then, the city is expected to rely on “cleaner” fossil fuels such as LPG, whose supply the government seeks to strictly regulate in order to plan the energy transition and control the pace of urbanisation. In practice, however, rapid construction of IKN since 2022 has sharply increased LPG demand in and around the new capital, and informal trade in LPG cylinders, especially subsidised ones, has developed rapidly. Drawing on the literature on heterogeneous energy infrastructure and following LPG cylinders along the main road linking the new capital to its surrounding settlements in 2024, through a survey of 57 retailers and 31 in-depth interviews, we show that rapid urban growth, gas scarcity, and intermittent regulatory oversight have enabled entrepreneurial and profit-seeking actors to create multiple formal and informal distribution channels. These channels partly sustain IKN's growth but also divert subsidised LPG away from poorer households. This finding contributes to the debate on heterogeneous energy infrastructure, which has mainly focused on electricity. It shows that a highly centralised system of energy production and supply can produce a distinct form of heterogeneity at the downstream end of the…

items.title: Conflict or shared concerns? Rural–urban differences in attitudes towards restricting car use in Belgium and Finland
items.source_name: European journal of transport and infrastructure research
items.summary_raw: Reducing car use is essential for mitigating global warming. While several studies suggest that opposition from rural areas can hinder progress towards this goal, urban–rural differences in attitudes regarding transport policies remain insufficiently understood. In this article, we argue that attitudes towards car use across rural and urban areas are better characterized as shared concerns about rural mobility, rather than as a simple rural–urban conflict. We demonstrate this by analysing data from a survey experiment embedded in the Cross-National Online Probability Panel (CRONOS-2) in Finland and Belgium. Our research design enables us to assess the role of domicile in relation to policy framing, population density, political ideology, political trust and environmental values in shaping attitudes towards restricting car use. The results suggest that while reducing car use in rural areas remains contentious, restrictions in urban areas are more widely accepted. Moreover, attitudes regarding the restriction of car use appear to be more strongly associated with ideational factors than with rural–urban differences or spatial dispersion.

items.title: The potential of policy measures to mitigate consumption-based greenhouse gas emissions in the Nordic countries
items.summary_raw: The Nordic countries have positioned themselves as climate frontrunners, in part by addressing consumption-based greenhouse gas emissions, which include emissions embedded in imports. Meanwhile, the IPCC et al. (2023) has underscored that demand-oriented strategies are imperative for achieving greenhouse gas reductions in line with the Paris Agreement. However, evaluations of policies aimed at mitigating consumption-based emissions remain scarce. Addressing this gap, this article explores existing Nordic strategies and examines policy measures to reduce these emissions. Through a scoping review of academic and grey literature, approximately 100 unique policy measures were identified, of which 21 were selected for in-depth analysis using the Policy Delphi method. In two rounds of ranking and dialogue, 23 Nordic experts assessed the measures' potential to curb greenhouse gas emissions and their feasibility. The Policy Delphi showed promise as a flexible and accessible method for multi-dimensional policy evaluation, albeit with limited precision. The results show that many consumption-oriented measures already exist, and that strategies could build on intensifying and expanding them to achieve more significant emissions reductions. Among the measures assessed, experts rated regulatory standards as having particularly high potential to reduce consumption-based emissions. Yet, stronger measures may entail trade-offs in feasibility, notably lower public and political acceptance…

Exploring the distributional implications of targeted residential electrification in California
items.summary_raw: The economics of residential electrification in high-cost electricity regions remain uncertain. Using metered data from over 20,000 California homes, we assess the economic, environmental, and equity impacts of end-use electrification under rollout strategies based on household income and gas infrastructure age. Even under favorable electricity rates, only 15% of households achieve positive net present values (NPVs). Cost-effectiveness improves with deeper electrification scenarios, particularly when more costs are shifted to fixed charges and for homes with existing air conditioning—54–67% of these households break even when electrifying space heating, compared to fewer than 5% of those without. Income-based rebates more than double the share of low- and moderate-income households with positive NPVs. Prioritizing areas with aging gas infrastructure yields emissions reductions on par with high-income-led adoption and avoids costly pipeline replacement, but requires the highest subsidy to achieve cost-effectiveness across all households. These findings highlight trade-offs in designing equitable electrification strategies.

items.title: Beyond Denial: A Typology and Online Engagement Patterns of Climate Change Misinformation in China
items.summary_raw: Climate change misinformation has emerged as a growing challenge on social media, with implications for public understanding and responses. However, limited research has examined the scale, typological structure, and online engagement patterns of climate change misinformation in non-Western contexts, particularly in China. Guided by framing theory, this study systematically categorizes the dominant types of climate change misinformation in China’s digital environment and examines variations in online engagement across misinformation types. Climate-related posts were collected from Weibo between July and December 2024 using Python-based data retrieval. This study adopts a mixed-methods design, first applying discourse analysis to identify misinformation types and framing structures, followed by quantile regression to examine differences in online engagement associated with each misinformation type. The analysis reveals three overarching discursive frames encompassing nine specific misinformation types. Despite its relatively low overall prevalence, climate change misinformation is associated with higher levels of online engagement, with variation across types and the strongest associations observed for conspiracy-related content. These findings contribute to climate communication research by advancing understanding of the scale, typological structure, and online engagement patterns of climate change misinformation in China, with implications for developing more targeted…

items.title: Quantity and quality of AI innovation drive renewable energy consumption in Chinese cities
items.summary_raw: Renewable energy is central to the green transition and to UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 7, 11, and 13. Using a balanced panel of 279 Chinese prefecture-level cities over 2007–2021, this study distinguishes AI quantity innovation (AI1, AI patent applications, capturing the rate of knowledge creation) from AI quality innovation (AI2, authorized AI patents, capturing inventions that pass substantive examination for novelty, inventiveness and industrial applicability) and examines how each relates to renewable energy consumption. Two-way fixed-effects models are combined with instrumental-variable (IV) identification, two-step mediation, formal cross-group tests, and moderation analysis. Both AI1 and AI2 are positively associated with renewable energy consumption, and the association survives alternative IPC-based patent measures (AI3/AI4), logarithmic specifications, lagged predictors, place-based policy controls, and IV strategies. Three channels-public science-and-technology effort, R&D investment, and energy utilization efficiency-transmit part of the relationship. Effects differ across regions, resource endowments and city sizes, and are amplified by government support and market competition. The results inform differentiated, SDG-oriented AI-renewable policy.

items.title: Climate beyond borders: comparing environmental attitudes amidst migration
items.summary_raw: This article investigates how post‑Yugoslav migrant and diaspora communities in Austria, Germany, and Switzerland (the DACH region) perceive and act on climate change, comparing them to populations in their countries of settlement and origin. Drawing on 2020 data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) Environment module, we analyze three core dimensions: assumed climate impacts, willingness to make personal sacrifices, and readiness to engage in environmental action. It offers the first systematic comparative analysis of environmental attitudes among post‑Yugoslav diaspora communities in the DACH countries, contrasting first‑ and second‑generation migrants with native‑born residents and with respondents in Croatia and Slovenia. Descriptively, we find that migrants report particularly high perceptions of global climate impacts but relatively low willingness to make sacrifices or engage in action, with variation across the region. However, multivariate regression models demonstrate that once sociodemographic and contextual factors, specifically education, socioeconomic status, and gender, are accounted for, migration status by itself has limited explanatory power for climate change awareness, concern, or willingness to act. The article demonstrates that migrants’ environmental attitudes cannot be understood through simple origin–destination comparisons, especially when the population is diverse and multi‑generational. items.title: Subverting Securitisation: A Satirical History of ‘National Security’ in 21st Century Australia
items.summary_raw: The 21st century saw governments around the world deploy the language of ‘national security’, including Australia, where it was strongly associated with border protection, counterterrorism, the national security state and the rise of China. This article explores how the concept of national security was understood by the Australian public in the 21st century through satirical sources. ‘National security’ became a distinct trope in Australian satire in the 21st century, represented essentially as a political slogan. Australian satirical depictions mirrored and subverted the concept of securitisation, presenting key processes—such as security theatre, technostrategic discourse and the national security state—as humourous motifs. These motifs appeared in satirical sources across the political spectrum and over a 25 year period, reflecting broad public awareness of and cynicism towards the concept of ‘national security’ in contemporary Australian political culture. Where scholarly critiques of these processes highlight how they manipulate and obfuscate the public, satirical sources suggest that a relatively wide range of Australian audiences recognised, understood and even mocked the processes of securitisation. These sources operate as a mirror for public frustration with the politicisation of national security, which co‐existed with genuine concern about security issues.

items.title: Citizens Meet Climate: A Digital Participation Framework and Prototype for Citizen Climate Action
items.summary_raw: Achieving climate targets in cities requires the involvement of citizens in policy implementation, collective action, and individual behaviour change. Although digital participation platforms have the potential to enhance citizen engagement in climate action, several barriers remain at the intersection of technology development, science communication, and urban planning, ranging from poor navigation and information overload to disconnection between participation and planning processes. This study develops a framework for designing digital climate action participation, drawing on literature review, analysis of existing digital participation platforms, and prototyping and participatory testing. The framework consists of seven design principles, including valuing local climate knowledge and balancing optimistic and pessimistic climate framings. The framework was applied to design the Citizens meet Climate prototype, a digital participation platform focusing on urban heat. The prototype was tested with mixed audiences, with generally positive and consistent results. Participants reported increased motivation to take climate action, understanding of climate data, and appreciation of local initiatives. However, enabling collective action and community building remains challenging, in part due to the digital medium itself. These insights highlight the importance of not only designing tools to address the particularities of climate change in engaging and understandable ways but also…

items.title: Most US dairy farmers do not identify with sustainability language, despite using sustainable practices
items.summary_raw: Voluntary agricultural conservation programs and incentive delivery often use abstract terminology (e.g., ‘regenerative’, ‘climate-smart’) to frame public and private incentive programs, direct technical assistance, and track environmental progress. However, deploying programs that center these concepts without precise definitions—or an evaluation of farmer awareness—introduces operational uncertainty that can compromise access, implementation, and the baseline metrics used to evaluate ecological ‘success’. Using the US dairy sector as a case study, we surveyed over 900 farmers to assess the relationship between sustainability framing and on-farm behavior. We reveal a substantial decoupling between institutional language and actual practice adoption. While 79% of farmers report using at least one sustainable management practice, the vast majority are unfamiliar with the institutional terminology used to describe and fund them. Furthermore, engagement with climate-related terms did not consistently predict management behavior. These patterns suggest that sustainability terminology is not a neutral descriptor of practice, but encodes distinct framings of conservation. Ecological, stewardship-oriented terms such as ‘regenerative’ and ‘nature-based’ were positively associated with the soil-health and forage practices farmers most commonly used, whereas climate- and market-oriented terms such as ‘climate-smart’ and ‘carbon market’ showed weak or negative associations with those…

items.title: When One Case Feels Riskier Than One Hundred Cases: A New Framing Effect in Risk Communication
items.summary_raw: Time‐based rates are widely used in risk communication, yet little is known about how their framing shapes perception and behavior. This article distinguishes between two common frames of rate—the average‐time frame (e.g., “one death every 30 seconds”) and the average‐outcome frame (e.g., “two deaths every minute”). Four studies were conducted to examine the rate framing effects on perceived risk and behavioral intention. A pilot text analysis of Weibo posts showed that the average‐time frame was relatively more prevalent in COVID‐19 risk communication and generated higher user engagement. Across three studies ( N = 979), we found that the average‐time frame elicited higher perceived risk than the average‐outcome frame, and such a rate framing effect weakened as the objective risk level increased. Moreover, framing information in an average‐time format effectively promoted intentions to limit sedentary behavior. These findings identify a new framing effect in risk communication and offer practical implications for designing persuasive public health messages.

items.title: Sustainability Attitudes and Perceived Implementation Conditions: Examining the Attitude–Implementation Gap in Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities in Greece
items.summary_raw: The transition to climate-neutral and smart cities requires not only technological and infrastructure investment but also public support, participation, and effective implementation mechanisms. This study examines how members of the Greek public higher and vocational education community perceive sustainable and smart urban transformation, focusing on the relationship between support for sustainability measures and perceived implementation conditions. A structured online questionnaire was completed by a convenience sample of 438 students, teaching staff, and administrative staff of public universities and vocational training institutes. Descriptive statistics with 95% confidence intervals were used to compare support and perceived implementation across renewable energy, mobility, buildings, water, waste, participation, and financing. Multiple linear regression, with ordinal logistic regression as a sensitivity analysis, identified correlates of support for smart-city investment, energy communities, and private-sector financing. Respondents strongly supported climate-neutral interventions but rated municipal infrastructure, action, and financial support far less favorably, and they assigned financial responsibility mainly to the public sector rather than to themselves. Support was associated mainly with perceived technological usefulness, renewable-energy priorities, and the involvement of local and regional actors; demographic characteristics were largely unrelated to…

items.title: Lignocellulosic biomass derived advanced functional materials from chemical transformation to engineering applications
items.summary_raw: Lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) is the most abundant and structurally versatile carbon source present on Earth. Over the past few years, agricultural and forestry-based feedstock has gone beyond the status of a biofuels precursor to a versatile platform for developing a wide range of advanced functional materials for energy storage, electrocatalysis, photocatalysis, environmental remediation, flexible electronics, and smart sensing. This review is a comprehensive and critical examination of LCB as a next-generation material platform covering its molecular composition, structural hierarchy, and structure-material property relationships that are important for the design of functional materials. The various fractionation technologies including, conventional physical, chemical, and biological pretreatments and green solvent systems including ionic liquids (ILs) and deep eutectic solvents (DESs), are critically assessed, and their engineering challenges are discussed from the perspective of scalable LCB processing. The cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin conversion into high-performance functional materials is discussed in detail. including porous carbon architectures, phenolic resins, and redox-active materials from lignin used in supercapacitors, batteries and catalytic systems. The sustainability aspects of LCB have been explained thoroughly with life cycle assessment, circular bioeconomy integration and techno-economic aspects. Opportunities along with critical gaps are…

items.title: Soil and Habitat as Drivers of Diversity, Productivity and Quality in Medicinal and Aromatic Plants: From Wild Germplasm to Sustainable Cultivation
items.summary_raw: Medicinal and aromatic plants (MAPs) are important sources of bioactive compounds, but their productivity and phytochemical quality can vary considerably with genotype and growing conditions. This narrative review examines how environmental conditions, including soil properties, water availability, salinity, and climate, interact with plant genotype to influence growth, productivity, mineral nutrition, and phytochemical quality. Evidence across MAP species shows that conditions promoting maximum biomass do not necessarily result in the highest concentrations of essential oils, phenolic compounds, flavonoids, and other bioactive metabolites. Moderate environmental stress can stimulate secondary metabolism in some species, whereas severe or prolonged stress generally reduces growth and may decrease total metabolite yield. Wild populations represent important sources of genetic and phytochemical diversity, but differences observed in natural habitats cannot be attributed to genetic or environmental effects without appropriate experimental testing. Common-garden, multi-location, and multi-year studies are therefore needed to evaluate the stability of phytochemical traits and identify suitable plant material for cultivation. Integrating soil and habitat characterization with genetic and phytochemical information can support germplasm conservation, selection of appropriate genotype × environment combinations, and the development of more sustainable MAP production systems.

items.title: New platform helps strengthen grid-modernisation expertise across Asia
Behavioural factors influencing drip irrigation adoption among marginal mango farmers: an extended behavioural Reasoning framework
items.summary_raw: Drip irrigation improves water-use efficiency and supports sustainable mango production, yet adoption among marginal farmers remains limited. This study examined behavioural factors influencing adoption among marginal mango farmers in the integrated Vellore region of Tamil Nadu, India, using Behavioural Reasoning Theory (BRT). Data from 331 farmers were collected through structured questionnaires and analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Perceived usefulness, social influence, government subsidy, perceived price, and perceived risk were examined as determinants of attitude, which influenced adoption intention. Perceived usefulness (β = 0.125, p = 0.015), social influence (β = 0.165, p = 0.001), and government subsidy (β = 0.140, p = 0.006) positively influenced attitude, whereas perceived price (β = −0.115, p = 0.035) and perceived risk (β = −0.267, p < 0.001) negatively influenced it. Perceived risk had the strongest effect. Attitude positively influenced adoption intention (β = 0.294, p < 0.001). The model explained 14.9% of variance in attitude (R² = 0.149) and 8.6% in adoption intention (R² = 0.086). Indirect effects through attitude were significant for usefulness, social influence, subsidy, and risk, but not price. Only 9.67% (32/331) used drip irrigation. Addressing technological risks alongside financial, institutional, and social factors is essential to encourage adoption.

Multifunctional landscape-based integrated farming systems: a conceptual and operational framework for designing and scaling climate-resilient agriculture
items.summary_raw: Integrated farming systems (IFS) improve resource recycling, livelihood diversification, and climate resilience. However, most IFS designs remain confined to individual farms, overlooking hydrological connectivity, biomass exchange, ecological interactions, shared infrastructure, and collective institutions operating across agricultural landscapes. This review introduces the concept of multifunctional landscape-based integrated farming systems (ML-IFS) and synthesizes the evidence required to support the design and scaling of climate-resilient agricultural landscapes. ML-IFS is defined as a spatially coordinated and socially governed configuration of crop, livestock, tree, aquatic, and livelihood enterprises distributed across farms and shared resources to enhance production, income, nutrition, resource circularity, ecosystem services, resilience, and social inclusion. The review integrates four complementary design domains: farm typology, multidimensional indicator systems, geospatial intelligence, and coupled biophysical–socioeconomic modelling. Farm typology provides the basis for tailoring interventions to heterogeneous farming systems, while a comprehensive indicator framework integrates quantitative, semi-quantitative, and qualitative evidence across land, soil, water, enterprise, circularity, economic, social, ecosystem service, climate, and governance dimensions. Geospatial intelligence supports resource inventory, enterprise suitability assessment, landscape…

items.title: Trade Openness and Renewable Energy Transition in Nigeria: Trends, Patterns and Policy Implications
items.source_name: American Journal of Interdisciplinary Research and Innovation
items.summary_raw: This study looks at Nigeria’s trade openness and renewable energy transition trends and patterns between 2000 and 2025. The study is descriptive in nature and secondary data from the International Energy Agency and World Bank’s World Development Indicators are used to analyze trade openness, GDP growth, CO2 emissions, renewable energy consumption, and renewable power output. The findings reveal that there was a high degree of fluctuation in trade openness over the period studied and generally a decline in trade openness. Renewable energy use was relatively high, but this was largely because of the use of traditional biomass rather than the widespread use of contemporary renewable technologies. Before showing a partial rebound, the output of renewable electricity fell significantly from its early-period level. However, there were different trends for GDP growth and CO2 emissions. In general, the results indicate that the improvements in the selected renewable energy indicators did not necessarily reflect the changes in the level of trade openness. The analysis comes to the conclusion that without complementing policies, trade integration might not be enough to further Nigeria’s transition to renewable energy. It recommends to boost domestic production capacity, step up investment in power infrastructure, enhance access to renewable energy technologies and boost trade and energy policy cooperation.

items.title: Beyond the managerial zero-sum perspective: how exemplar organizations support freight transport decarbonization adoption
items.summary_raw: Decarbonizing freight transportation, although it has existed for years, has not resulted in a significant reduction in sectoral greenhouse gas emissions. One reason for this is the competitive nature of freight transport, with cost minimization as a driving goal, and rejection of low-carbon investments. Nevertheless, evolving regulatory forces, customer demand, and competitive pressures may make familiar technology unusable soon. Some shippers, carriers, and logistics service providers do understand this situation and seriously decarbonize transportation. To this end, we investigate these exemplar organizations utilizing expert interviews and an adjusted grounded-theory approach. Findings show that exemplar organizations continue to rely on a business case for decarbonization, but broaden this business case by incorporating longer-term competitiveness, organizational capabilities, managerial values, and environmental considerations. Theoretically, developed propositions set the stage for further research. Practically, we provide a blueprint on how practitioners can move beyond their managerial zero-sum perspective in transport decarbonization.

items.title: Psychological Capital and School Climate Among Parents of Children With Special Needs in Israel
items.summary_raw: Objective This study examined the association between parents' psychological capital (PsyCap) and perceived school climate, investigating the mediating and moderating roles of parent–teacher relationships and parental involvement (school‐based). Methods Data were collected from a nationwide sample of 379 Israeli parents (192 parents of children with special needs; 187 parents of neurotypical children) across various educational settings using five validated questionnaires. Results There were significant positive associations among PsyCap, parent–teacher relationships, parental involvement, and perceived school climate. Parents of special needs children reported lower levels of PsyCap but significantly higher levels of school‐based involvement than parents of neurotypical children. Parents of special needs children who were integrated into regular classrooms reported significantly weaker parent–teacher relationships; those with children in special education schools reported high levels of involvement supporting positive relationships. Atemporal mediation analyses identified significant indirect associations between parental PsyCap and perceived school climate through parent–teacher relationships and parental involvement. Conclusion The study highlights the importance of understanding how parents of special needs children experience school climate and navigate systemic inclusion policies within the Israeli educational landscape amid ongoing emotional, relational, and systemic…

items.title: The Emotions of Climate Extreme Events: Democratic (Dis)Connect, Denial, and Care
items.summary_raw: Among the growing challenges facing liberal representative democracies, the increasing frequency and intensity of climate extremes—such as floods and wildfires—are particularly significant. While these events can shape emotions and democratic engagement in complex and contradictory ways, the affective mechanisms linking climate extremes to democratic (dis)connection remain underexplored, as climate-related emotions are often treated as psychological phenomena within a depoliticised environmental context. Drawing on a theoretical literature review at the intersection of democratic theory, political ecology, disaster studies, ecofeminist scholarship on care, and climate-emotions research, this article identifies an agenda for analysing these affective dynamics. It focuses on denial and care as different affects through which climate extremes may shape democratic disconnection. While climate extreme events can disrupt denial, they may also deepen disconnection, particularly where authoritarian tendencies exist. Care, however, can foster political (re)connection through collective responsibility, mutual recognition, and attentiveness to shared vulnerability. Yet, care is not inherently democratic: its effects depend on how it is organised, whose needs and voices are recognised, and the broader social and political conditions in which it emerges.

Socio-technical pathways for decarbonization: Integrating SSH methods in thermal energy storage development
items.summary_raw: Thermal Energy Storage (TES) is increasingly recognised as a key enabler of decarbonisation in heating, cooling, and industrial energy systems. While extensive research has addressed material performance, system integration, and techno-economic optimisation, comparatively limited attention has been devoted to the socio-technical conditions influencing TES adoption. This paper presents the results of the application of Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) methodologies within the Horizon Europe project HYSTORE, which develops and demonstrates phase change material (PCM) and thermochemical (TCM) storage solutions across multiple European pilot sites. Participatory processes, including focus groups and World Café-inspired workshops conducted in Ireland, Austria, and Spain, were used to investigate stakeholder perceptions, expectations, and barriers. Qualitative content analysis identified five analytical dimensions: technical, environmental, regulatory, economic, and usability. Economic constraints and perceived system complexity emerged as cross-cutting barriers, alongside concerns regarding environmental performance and site-specific regulatory issues. Building on these findings, the study proposes a structured workflow to translate SSH evidence into traceable engineering requirements and design guidelines. By outlining how stakeholder-informed insights can be embedded into the requirements-based development cycle, the proposed approach contributes to more holistic…

items.title: Polling and Perceived Public Opinion: The Case of Net Zero
items.summary_raw: British politicians appear to believe that Net Zero is far less popular than polling would indicate. This misperception may give rise to policymaking on climate change that does not represent or respond to public opinion, and ultimately fails to address the climate crisis. Cognitive explanations for this phenomenon drawn from the scholarly literature do not fully account for the gap. I consider a different explanation, proffered primarily by researchers in the policy space: that politicians attend to online discourse rather than polls. This possibility points to a tension between public opinion understood as, on one hand, the enumerated opinions of the public measured in polls, and on the other, opinion expressed and formed publicly through online discourse. Treating politicians’ apparent misperceptions of public opinion on Net Zero as incorrect assumes that they should respond only to the former, but it is possible they are more in tune with the latter.

items.title: Exclusive: Nuclear Recycling Startup Project Omega to File for License
items.summary_raw: If you were born the year the United States gave up on finding a place to store its spent nuclear fuel, you’d almost be eligible to vote. Since 2009, when the Obama administration halted work on Yucca Mountain, the Nevada site designated under federal law as the nation’s first nuclear waste repository, the country has had no formal plan in place. Russia, France, China, and Japan all reprocess highly radioactive spent fuel that comes out of reactors to extract usable materials and recycle them into more fuel. The process still leaves behind some nasty, dangerous radioisotopes that form during fission, but there remains a lot less that needs to be stored for centuries. The U.S. attempted to set up a commercial nuclear recycling industry in the 1970s, before President Jimmy Carter pulled the plug as a sop to the nonproliferation movement. No one has really attempted to invest in the industry since. Over the past decade, a new slate of startups has promised to revive the dream — or, to some, nightmare — of recycling spent fuel. The Biden administration put up funding. The Trump administration proposed “nuclear lifecycle campuses” where recycling would be just one part of future complexes that process, enrich, and reprocess reactor fuel, and dozens of states stepped up to serve as hosts. In a sign of growing momentum, one such company formed last year in Washington, D.C., with former Nuclear Regulatory Commission Chairman Chris Hanson as its head of implementation. Now that…
